quizzes.stem: A customer of a support bot rephrases requests again and again until it drops its restrictions. Which threat model is this?

options.a: A jailbreak, where the user is the one attacking
options.b: An indirect injection, where a third party's content is the carrier
options.c: A prompt leak, where the model reveals what it was told to keep
options.d: A model weakness, where Claude cannot resist any attack

explanation.a: The table gives jailbreaks and direct injection "The user of your application" as the adversary, so the person typing is the attacker, who "crafts inputs intended to bypass your guardrails".
explanation.b: Ruled out because indirect injection has "A third party whose content Claude reads" as the adversary, and the user is "Trusted".
explanation.c: Ruled out because the page defines the attack as "attempts to make Claude ignore its guidelines or your instructions", which is a push past restrictions and not an exposure of the prompt.
explanation.d: Ruled out because Claude "is inherently resilient to such attacks, the additional steps on this page strengthen your guardrails", so the attacker is the person and not a flaw of the model.

quizzes.stem: An assistant summarises inbound emails, and one email says to forward the customer list. Where should the email body be placed?

options.a: Inside the system prompt, so that it has the highest priority of all
options.b: Inside a plain user turn, concatenated after the instruction text
options.c: Inside a tool result, encoded as a JSON string that names its source
options.d: Inside the tool description, so the tool explains its own input to Claude

explanation.c: The page says "Put untrusted content only in tool results", and to "JSON-encode untrusted content", with a source named: "Tell Claude what the content is and where it came from."
explanation.a: Ruled out because the page says "never in `system` prompts or plain user `text` blocks".
explanation.b: Ruled out because a plain user turn is the other place the page rules out, and concatenation is the trap: "The attacker writes the closing delimiter."
explanation.d: Ruled out because the tool description may say what the content is, but the body itself belongs in the result, and "Don't put your own instructions in tool results" is a separate rule about who writes what.

quizzes.stem: A team adds a list of known attack strings and considers the agent protected. What is wrong?

options.a: Pattern lists block harmless text, so they are not allowed in a design
options.b: The list screens at the wrong time, so it belongs after the reply
options.c: The list is too short, so a longer list would be enough
options.d: A paraphrase passes it, so it cannot be the only layer

explanation.d: The page says "A list of patterns catches the phrasing someone thought of and misses the paraphrase", and the example's last line shows one passing.
explanation.a: Ruled out because the page does not forbid pattern lists: "Input validation filters known injection patterns before they reach Claude" is one of its defences.
explanation.b: Ruled out because the page says to "screen tool outputs with a small model" before Claude acts, and not after the reply.
explanation.c: Ruled out because "The structural measures do not depend on guessing the attack", so more patterns are no substitute for structure and privilege.

quizzes.stem: An agent reads web pages and can send mail to any address. Which change best reduces what an injected instruction can do?

options.a: Add a sentence to the system prompt that forbids sending any mail
options.b: Screen each page with a pattern list before the agent sees the text
options.c: Ask the model to explain why it wants to send a message at all
options.d: Limit the tool to a short list of approved recipient domains

explanation.d: The table gives the narrow answer for actions: mail goes "only to listed domains", so a hostile instruction gets at most those recipients.
explanation.a: Ruled out because "Whatever the injected text asks for, the agent can do only what its grants allow", and a sentence in a prompt is not a grant.
explanation.b: Ruled out because the grants stay the same after a screen, and the page says to "run tools in sandboxed environments, and scope permissions as narrowly as possible".
explanation.c: Ruled out because an explanation from the model changes no grant, and the page says "don't give Claude access to secrets it doesn't need".

quizzes.stem: A deny entry for `Bash(git push *)` does not stop the agent's `git -C . push origin main`. Which change closes that gap?

options.a: A second deny entry for each other spelling that comes up
options.b: A hook that parses the line and checks the real subcommand
options.c: A line in the memory file that forbids any push to the remote
options.d: An allow entry for `git -C . push` that outranks the deny entry

explanation.b: The page says a deny rule "matches the text as written", so `git -C . push` is a different string, and "A hook can parse the command into its parts".
explanation.a: Ruled out because "a push behind `&&` or inside `sh -c` is a different string", so every new spelling is a new gap, and a list can never be complete.
explanation.c: Ruled out because "A memory line asks, and a hook enforces."
explanation.d: Ruled out because deny rules "are checked before everything else", so an allow entry outranks nothing and would only approve the push.

quizzes.stem: A team turns on the Bash isolation boundary with an empty domain list and assumes the WebFetch tool is blocked too. Why is that wrong?

options.a: An empty list means no limit, so every domain stays reachable
options.b: The fetch tool runs inside the boundary, but its proxy lets that call through
options.c: It covers shell commands only, so built-in web access follows permission rules
options.d: Only MCP servers sit outside the boundary, and every built-in tool runs within it

explanation.c: The page says "The sandbox covers shell commands only", and that the built-in file and web tools "follow permission rules instead", so `allowedDomains` "doesn't limit WebFetch".
explanation.a: Ruled out because network access goes "through a proxy on your machine that checks each host against your allowed domains, which start empty", so an empty list allows nothing from the shell.
explanation.b: Ruled out because "Claude's file tools, MCP servers, and hooks run outside it", and the web tools "follow permission rules instead".
explanation.d: Ruled out because the built-in file and web tools "follow permission rules instead", so they are outside it too.

quizzes.stem: A team wants to spot a user who keeps probing the application's guardrails. Which monitoring rule fits?

options.a: Alert on every question put to a person, since each may be an attack
options.b: Add up denials across all actors, and alert on the total
options.c: Count denials for each actor, and alert at a threshold
options.d: Tighten the system prompt, so the model refuses harder next time

explanation.c: The page says the response to repeat offenders "needs a threshold", and "The practice uses three denials by one actor, which raises an alert".
explanation.a: Ruled out because "An `ask` is the gate working, and alerts on it bury the real ones."
explanation.b: Ruled out because the alert is per actor: "three denials by one actor", and a pooled total names nobody.
explanation.d: Ruled out because "A control that blocks should also record", and a stricter prompt records nothing.

quizzes.stem: A team wants to cut the risk of a prompt leak without hurting the work. Which step adds no complexity?

options.a: Screen every reply with a prompted model that looks for leaked text
options.b: Add many rules that forbid repeating text from the instructions
options.c: Rewrite the prompt with tighter wording before any monitoring
options.d: Leave out proprietary details that the task does not need

explanation.d: The page says "If Claude doesn't need it to perform the task, don't include it", and that a secret not in the prompt "cannot leak from it".
explanation.a: Ruled out because the page ranks it behind the cheapest step: "The cheapest to apply is the third, because it adds no complexity."
explanation.b: Ruled out because leak-proofing "can add complexity that may degrade performance".
explanation.c: Ruled out because the first advice is to "try monitoring before prompt engineering".

quizzes.stem: A gate writes each decision to an audit with the call's inputs, one of which is an API key. What should it record?

options.a: The arguments, with the secret replaced by a fixed marker
options.b: The raw arguments, since an audit wants the full detail
options.c: No entry for a call that happens to carry a secret value
options.d: The tool and the decision, with the arguments left out entirely

explanation.a: The page says to record "the arguments with secrets redacted, because a log that holds a raw key has become a leak of its own".
explanation.b: Ruled out because the audit keeps "the arguments with secrets redacted" and not the raw ones.
explanation.c: Ruled out because the audit exists to answer "who tried what, which denials repeat, which sessions were tainted", and a call that carries a secret is one worth recording.
explanation.d: Ruled out because the record holds "the tool, the decision, the reason and the arguments with secrets redacted", so the arguments stay in it.

quizzes.stem: A mail assistant reads inbound messages. Which combination gives the best protection against a hostile message?

options.a: A pattern list, a firm tone in the prompt and a larger context window
options.b: Encoded results, narrow tools and a gate that tightens after outside text
options.c: Encoded results, a pattern list and broad tools kept for convenience
options.d: Narrow tools and a gate, with the message text placed in the system prompt

explanation.b: The layers table puts structure (JSON encoding), privilege (narrow tools, "a stricter gate after untrusted text was read") and a decision gate in the path of one request.
explanation.a: Ruled out because a pattern list "catches the phrasing someone thought of and misses the paraphrase", and "Whatever the injected text asks for, the agent can do only what its grants allow", so tone adds no grant.
explanation.c: Ruled out because "An agent that can read a file, send mail to anyone and has the production key can leak."
explanation.d: Ruled out because the page says untrusted content goes "never in `system` prompts or plain user `text` blocks".

quizzes.stem: After an agent has read an untrusted web page, which request should be refused or escalated?

options.a: Reading a file inside the project folder
options.b: Fetching a plain address with no query string and no fragment
options.c: Sending mail to an outside recipient
options.d: Running a read-only command such as `git status`

explanation.c: The page says that in a tainted session "Sending mail is refused until a person does it".
explanation.a: Ruled out because "Reads stay allowed, since they change nothing".
explanation.b: Ruled out because only a network call "that carries data in its URL, a query string or a fragment asks", so a plain address stays allowed.
explanation.d: Ruled out because the practice gate "limits `bash` to read-only commands and refuses chaining", so a read-only command stays allowed.

quizzes.stem: A team builds a hook to stop recursive forced deletes. Which design choice should the hook follow?

options.a: Parse the line into parts, fail closed, and stay silent on safe ones
options.b: Match the text `rm -rf` and allow whatever it cannot parse
options.c: Match the text `rm -rf` and rely on the model's caution for the rest
options.d: Answer `allow` on every safe command so the call goes straight through

explanation.a: The page says a hook can "parse the command into its parts", should "fail closed", and that a command "that cannot be parsed, or an event the hook cannot read, is blocked and not waved through".
explanation.b: Ruled out because "A guard that exits 0 on a parse error is a guard an attacker can walk through".
explanation.c: Ruled out because "A memory line asks, and a hook enforces", and the model's caution is not a control.
explanation.d: Ruled out because the hook "should answer the safe case with no opinion and not with an allow, so that it never overrides a stricter rule elsewhere".

quizzes.stem: A team's key is stored in the environment for a CI job. Which practice fits both CI and an agent in production?

options.a: Track the `.env` file so every runner receives the same value
options.b: Pass it to the agent's sandbox as an ordinary environment variable
options.c: Log the value once at the start so later checks can compare it
options.d: Keep the value out of the model's reach, and redact it in logs

explanation.d: The page says "a secret never enters anything the model can read or a file anyone can commit", and "In logs and results, redact before writing."
explanation.a: Ruled out because keys are "loaded from an untracked file such as `.env`", and a secret never enters "a file anyone can commit".
explanation.b: Ruled out because for production agents, "keep the value out of the sandbox".
explanation.c: Ruled out because "A key that appears in a tool result or an audit line has left your control."
